doc.title: Frank Tiberi interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 30, 2022

title: Self-taught theory, teaching, and making money in jazz today
summary: Tiberi did not attend a jazz program; he teaches performing students and says he looks up to no one after Coltrane.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Okay. So I find it very interesting that you didn’t attend the jazz — the higher education jazz program is that correct?
So this is all your own initiative, your curiosity, and your musicality that has enabled this kind of theoretical knowledge?

Yes, yes, yes. Since I’ve been doing it actually I feel comfortable and I mean I do feel very comfortable even being able to really teach it to students that come in that pay money to be taught or so — but I mean these are performing students you know, the standard students that come in of course I mean they want to get away by doing the exams and of course I mean they’re doing other things other than playing jazz. But I do give them the same process. If they want to just play then I always say, “I know you’d like to be an arranger, you’re doing this and all that but you want to play, right?” So yeah the performing students, you know I pound a little more into them because you know I want them to get ahead real quick. And they are playing, at the age of 18 and 19. I’ve got some students that — pretty scary.
Are their saxophone Gods the same as yours? Like Coltrane died some 55 years ago. Who do they look up to?

Well I really don’t know because I don’t look up to anyone actually. You know my dear friends, I mean you know I think the inspiration that I got from him actually just you know hasn’t given me the interest to really hear — I hear everybody of course well I’m talking about really digging into any kind of solos that anybody plays. Right now you have players right now that are just maybe playing contrafacts and tunes and they’re you know playing, trying to get as much in as possible. But you know it’s nice to hear them but I don’t really get right into them actually.
What makes for — in your definition, your personal definition, when does somebody become an innovator in the jazz lexicon?

Well I don’t know what you mean by that question. I mean — I mean everybody really does want to make a CD, they want to really be heard. Of course I mean YouTube is hot right now. It’s unbelievable that you can hear so many players on YouTube. I guess their
interest is to be coming that way, to be able to get gigs and I guess get into the stage of making the money. I suppose that would be it.
Right. Making the money in jazz.
